Neonates of the Smallthorn Skate emerge from their egg cases at a total length of 12 centimeters [Lb = 12 centimeters], a modest size that reflects the limited yolk reserves available during development. This species, like many deepwater skates, invests in a relatively small number of large, yolky eggs that undergo an extended incubation period. At a water temperature of 2 °C [T = 2 °C], the age at birth has been calculated at approximately 730 days [ab = approximately 730 days], a remarkably protracted embryonic phase that is among the longest documented for any skate species. This slow developmental pace is likely an adaptation to the cold, stable thermal conditions of the bathyal depths these animals inhabit. The extended time within the egg case allows for the development of a well-formed pup that is capable of benthic foraging immediately upon emergence, reducing the vulnerability associated with a tiny, poorly developed hatchling.

Female Bathyraja minispinosa ultimately attain a considerably larger body size than males, with the maximum recorded total length reaching 82.5 centimeters [Li = 82.5 centimeters]. This dimorphism in ultimate size is a common pattern among skates and is generally attributed to the energetic demands of egg production. Corresponding to this large skeletal frame, the maximum adult body mass for females has been estimated at 3,300 grams [Wwi = 3,300 grams], placing this species among the medium-bodied members of the genus Bathyraja. This maximum body mass is derived from length-weight regressions fitted to specimens collected during deepwater trawl surveys. The substantial body size of mature females likely confers a fecundity advantage, as larger body cavities can accommodate a greater number of developing eggs within the oviducal glands. These life-history traits point toward a k-selected strategy typical of many deep-sea elasmobranchs.

Sexual maturation in the Smallthorn Skate occurs at different sizes for each sex, reflecting divergent energetic priorities. Females reach puberty at a total length of 67.4 centimeters [Lp = 67.4 centimeters], whereas males achieve this milestone at a slightly larger size of 70.1 centimeters [Lp = 70.1 centimeters]. This pattern, where males mature at a greater length than females, is somewhat atypical among skates and may indicate that male-male competition for access to receptive females favors larger body size at the onset of reproductive activity. The onset of gonadal activity is associated with the development of claspers in males and the enlargement of the ovary and shell glands in females. These size-at-puberty estimates were derived from macroscopic examination of the reproductive tracts of individuals captured in the Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska, providing a robust dataset for characterizing the species' maturation schedule.

Reproductive output in Bathyraja minispinosa appears to be constrained by the cold temperatures of its environment. The maximum annual reproductive rate, observed under stable conditions at 2 °C [T = 2 °C], equates to females producing approximately 8 pups per year [Ri = approximately 8 pups per year]. This relatively low fecundity is consistent with the species' strategy of depositing large, well-yolked egg cases on the seafloor. Each egg case contains a single embryo, and the protracted 730-day incubation means that a female can only produce a limited number of offspring across her lifetime. The reproductive cycle likely involves a period of vitellogenesis followed by ovulation and subsequent egg case deposition, a process that may span several months for each batch of eggs. This slow reproductive tempo is a common feature among deepwater chondrichthyans and renders the species highly vulnerable to overexploitation.

The maximum lifespan of the Smallthorn Skate has been determined through vertebral banding analysis, indicating that individuals can reach an age of approximately 13,870 days [am = approximately 13,870 days] when living at 2 °C [T = 2 °C]. This extreme longevity, equivalent to roughly 38 years, is characteristic of slow-growing, late-maturing deep-sea fishes and underscores the species' low intrinsic rate of population increase. The combination of a delayed onset of reproduction, exceptionally low fecundity, and a very long lifespan places Bathyraja minispinosa at the slow extreme of the life-history continuum among skates. Such a strategy is viable only in environments where natural mortality rates are consistently low, a condition generally met in the cold, dark, and relatively predator-poor bathyal zone. Conservation concerns arise because any increase in mortality from fishing pressure will be compensated for only very slowly, if at all, given the species' demographic constraints.
